title: Property-based testing with Hypothesis
summary: Instead of picking examples, state a property that holds for every input and let Hypothesis search for a counterexample and shrink it: round-trips, invariants and comparisons with a simple model.

steps.title: Let the computer pick the inputs
body: Example tests check the cases you thought of. A **property** is a statement that must hold for *every* input, and **Hypothesis** generates hundreds of inputs to try to break it. When one fails, it **shrinks** the input to the smallest failing case and prints it:
from hypothesis import given, example, strategies as st
- **invariants**: the output is sorted, has the same length, never exceeds a cap, stays within a range;
- **a simple model**: the fast implementation agrees with an obviously-correct slow one.

Hypothesis remembers failing examples in a local `.hypothesis` folder and replays them first next time, so a failure found once keeps failing until fixed. The .NET equivalents are FsCheck (with `FsCheck.Xunit.v3`) and CsCheck.

items: `sorted(xs)` is in order and keeps every item

steps.prompt: Hypothesis reports `Falsifying example: test_total(items=[Item(price=0.1), Item(price=0.2)])` for a test asserting `total(items) == 0.3`. What did it find?
options: Binary floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so either the code should use Decimal or the property should compare with pytest.approx
That lists of two items are not supported
steps.explain: Shrinking turned some random failing list into the smallest one, which makes the cause obvious. Money belongs in `Decimal`; measurements compare with a tolerance.

steps.title: Properties for run-length encoding
prompt: `rle.py` compresses runs of letters: `encode("aaab")` is `"3a1b"`, `decode("3a1b")` is `"aaab"`.
while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]:

Write tests (`from rle import encode, decode`): at least **3**, including a Hypothesis **round-trip** property over letter strings (`st.text(alphabet="abcxyz")`) and an **invariant** (for example: the encoding never has two neighbouring runs of the same letter, or the counts add up to `len(s)`). Four planted bugs, one of which only shows on runs of 10 or more.
starter: from hypothesis import given, example, strategies as st
solution: from hypothesis import given, example, strategies as st
assert sum(int(n) for n in re.findall(r"\d+", encode(s))) == len(s)

target: while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]:

mutants.name: decode only reads one digit
mutants.hint: Runs of 10 or more need two digits: add @example("a" * 12) to your property.

hints: The round-trip is two lines: `@given(st.text(alphabet="abcxyz"))` and `assert decode(encode(s)) == s`.
Hypothesis will find most bugs on its own, but long runs are rare in random text: pin them with `@example("a" * 12)`.
An invariant: the numbers in `encode(s)` add up to `len(s)` (`re.findall(r"\d+", ...)`).
steps.explain: One property replaced dozens of examples, and `@example` makes sure the rare-but-important case (a run of two-digit length) is always tried. That combination, properties plus pinned examples, is how property testing is used at work.
